thumbnail.headline: Ask **first**?
thumbnail.sub: Elvis, Eminem rights holders vs. Suno

chapters.intro: Monologue: A pickup gets laid off, AI rewrites recipes
chapters.su-who: Main Course: AI learns to sing. Is that stealing?
chapters.af-intro: AI Fail: The hacking tool left unlocked

d9a2.text: This is Tech Signal, where we pick today's real signal out of all the noise.

hk01.text: Today's main course is a lawsuit: two music-rights groups sued AI music company Suno.

su05.text: But how is AI learning songs different from us learning from records?

su06.text: We'll argue it out in the main course.

hi03.text: First, two more stories since Friday.

ct01.text: First, last Friday, November 6, Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production around mid-2027.

ct02.text: The Cybertruck is Tesla's stainless-steel pickup.

ct03.text: Ending it? What about the owners?

ct04.text: Musk said the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time.

ct05.text: Reports don't mention parts or repairs afterward.

ct06.text: "Around for a long time" sounds a lot like a breakup's "let's stay friends."

ct07.text: For owners, that still beats "it's gone."

ct08.text: The goal is to free up Texas factory capacity for more Cybercabs.

ct09.text: The Cybercab is Tesla's robotaxi: two seats, no steering wheel, no pedals.

ct10.text: So the Cybertruck got laid off, and its replacement doesn't even have a steering wheel.

ct11.text: Even cars get automated out of a job!

ct12.text: And per numbers cited by Decrypt, Cybertruck sales are only about a tenth of what the line was built for.

ct13.text: A tenth? If that line were staff, it'd be job hunting.

ct14.text: Classic question time: so should I get a new phone?

ct15.text: No. This time, the pickup gets replaced.

ny01.text: Second, the New York Times recipe app, NYT Cooking, just added an AI assistant.

ny02.text: It rewrites recipes around what you have.

ny03.text: So it builds a dish from my leftovers?

ny04.text: Basically, as a new version. The original stays.

ny05.text: At launch, it's only for subscribers on iOS.

ny06.text: On Saturday, November 7, a Verge reporter posted a test with chicken tenders, rice and green beans.

ny07.text: In seconds, it made a new recipe, title and all.

ny08.text: She also threw a curveball: could trifle, a layered dessert, swap its ladyfingers for ground beef?

ny09.text: It said no ground beef anywhere in a dessert.

ny10.text: That may be the AI industry's best-held line today.

ny11.text: Finally, an AI that tells humans no!

ny18.text: And the front it held was dessert.

ny12.text: But you can't save the new version separately.

ny13.text: Baking the original, she asked about butter and got the edited amount, unlabeled.

ny14.text: So she almost baked the other recipe's cake?

ny15.text: She said that much would make the cake dry.

ny16.text: I think it's handy. At least the original's safe.

ny17.text: Half agree: she says check amounts and times against the original.

su01.text: Third is today's main course: according to a Verge report on Sunday, November 8, Suno has been sued again.

su07.text: OK, let's fight: how is AI learning to sing different?

su03.text: One group suing Suno holds the music rights of Elvis Presley; the other is the publisher of several of Eminem's biggest records.

su04.text: Both say Suno illegally mimics these singers' music and lyrics.

mc04.text: So the plaintiffs may not be the singers.

mc01.text: Imagine typing one line for old-school rock, and seconds later, a new song.

mc02.text: That's what Suno does: you type text, it generates music and lyrics.

mc05.text: I'll pick a side first: I'm with AI.

mc06.text: AI learns music like we did from records. Everyone grows up on the greats.

mc07.text: I'm on the other side: their songs, their voices.

mc08.text: And the plaintiffs say Suno had no license.

mc09.text: First, the Presley case: the lawyers say Suno violated a Tennessee state law called the ELVIS Act.

mc10.text: Per The Verge, this law bars AI companies from copying a singer's voice without consent.

mc11.text: The law's full name is the Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act, ELVIS for short.

mc12.text: So the law is named after Elvis?

mc13.text: The report doesn't say. Only that it spells ELVIS.

mc14.text: Still, a law whose acronym spells ELVIS is now actually being used to sue over Elvis's songs.

mc15.text: As for the Eminem publisher's case, the report doesn't say which law it uses.

mc16.text: So for that one, we know they sued, just not with what.

mc17.text: I still think it's unfair to AI. What singer didn't grow up on their idols?

mc18.text: People can imitate Elvis, so why can't AI?

mc20.text: It says what takes people years to learn and hone, Suno copies in seconds, unlicensed.

mc21.text: What about impersonators? Do tribute singers get sued too?

mc22.text: Impersonators at least use their own throats.

mc23.text: But they profit from copying too. It's not that different.

mc24.text: And this isn't Suno's first lawsuit.

mc25.text: According to The Verge, Suno already faces a pile of lawsuits, from big music companies like Sony and UMG.

mc27.text: Yep, Suno's lawsuits could fill a greatest-hits album.

mc32.text: As reported, the core of both cases is who Suno's output imitates.

mc33.text: So Kai, "learning" isn't the only issue here. "Sounding alike" is.

mc34.text: OK, but who decides what sounds alike?

mc35.text: A court decides. For now, it's just allegations.

mc36.text: To be fair, Suno did respond.

mc37.text: A Suno spokesperson said it helps people make original music, not trade on anyone's name or likeness.

mc03.text: The text a user types to an AI is called a prompt.

mc39.text: Suno bans specific singers' names and song titles in prompts.

mc40.text: It also uses outside vendors to screen uploaded audio and lyrics for misuse.

mc41.text: See? You can't even type a singer's name!

mc42.text: That's what it says. Nobody in the report tested it.

mc43.text: OK, one point to you. At least Suno can say how it blocks.

mc71.text: Savor it. It may be today's only one.

mc68.text: But if AI asks about every song, it'll never finish!

mc69.text: Then learn less, I'd say. No singer heard every record before debuting.

mc72.text: OK, enough about who's right. Now, money.

mc45.text: So where did the money go?

mc46.text: The plaintiffs say it went to Suno.

mc47.text: The complaint says Suno encoded artists' identity, effort, creativity and time.

mc48.text: And it turned all that into a nonstop cash conveyor belt.

mc49.text: So how much do they want?

mc50.text: The report doesn't say the damages or Suno's earnings.

mc51.text: The complaint says Suno wants human creativity obsolete.

mc52.text: But regular folks win: non-musicians can make songs!

mc53.text: More people making songs is good.

mc54.text: But the plaintiffs say Suno profits off others' names, unlicensed.

mc55.text: And Taiwan? Could its singers get AI versions too?

mc56.text: The report never mentions Taiwan or Asia.

mc57.text: And the Presley case uses a Tennessee state law, in the US.

mc58.text: So listeners in Taiwan can start by understanding this US case.

mc60.text: One: how courts view laws like the ELVIS Act that protect singers' voices.

mc61.text: One: I bet lots of lawyers get busy.

mc62.text: Two: which law the Eminem publisher's case actually uses.

mc63.text: Three: whether outsiders can verify Suno's safeguards.

mc64.text: My view: Kai's half right. Learning isn't the problem; humans do it too.

mc65.text: To profit off others' voices and fame, asking first is basic manners.

mc66.text: No idea how the court rules. For now, it's all allegations.

mc67.text: I'm still with AI. Learning isn't wrong. Asking first? Courts decide.

af01.text: OK, today's AI Fail stars an AI tool called Artex that hunts for weaknesses in computer systems on its own.

af02.text: On Friday, November 6, TechCrunch reported researchers found hundreds of Artex copies sitting on the open internet.

af04.text: Open source means public code anyone can download free.

af05.text: Does this matter to regular people?

af06.text: Yes. TechCrunch says since its public release in July, it's been linked to several real cyberattacks.

af07.text: Microsoft says a China-state-aligned hacker group used it from as early as September to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations.

af08.text: Then the fail: security firm Censys found over 800 Artex setups reachable from the web, with no password needed to log in.

af09.text: No password? Hacking tool, or public library?

af10.text: A weakness-hunting tool didn't set its own password.

af11.text: That's a locksmith hanging his master key outside!

af12.text: To be fair, researchers say not every copy was misused. Many are run by authorized testers.

af13.text: Authorized testing means a company hires attackers to find its holes first.

af14.text: But this software never needs to be online, so why hundreds are exposed is still unclear.

af32.text: Whoever's using it, leaving it online and unlocked is the problem.

af15.text: TechCrunch also says attack tools were exposed too.

af31.text: They include malware hidden in victims' networks.

af16.text: So even the armory is open for tours?

af18.text: Security firm CrowdStrike tied September attacks on South Korea's finance sector to a hacker using Artex.

af19.text: Part of the reason: the hacker left their Artex folder online for anyone to open.

af20.text: It's like a thief posting the heist plan online, set to public.

af21.text: Censys data shows it was public for months, and its attack data seemed to go beyond Korean banks.

af22.text: Even bad guys forget to lock up. Comforting.

af23.text: TechCrunch says many Artex-linked attacks used basic weaknesses, like weak passwords or no multi-factor authentication.

af24.text: Multi-factor authentication adds a second check beyond your password, like a phone code.

af25.text: Classic question: do I need a new phone?

af26.text: No, you need a new password.

af27.text: Artex later went closed; new versions are for paying clients.

af28.text: But dozens of copies of its code remain on code-sharing sites.

af29.text: Now it's locked, but the keys are long copied.

af30.text: Lesson: lock your own door first.

so01.text: Honestly, today's biggest story is Suno's two new lawsuits.

so02.text: I'm least sure which law the Eminem publisher's case uses. The report hasn't said.

so03.text: Today's most principled AI is the recipe bot refusing ground beef in dessert.

so04.text: If even a recipe AI can say no, I trust AI a little more.

so05.text: Today's full rundown is on Mokaair, with links in the description.

ou01.text: The plaintiffs say AI differs in license and speed.
